Lines to translate:
1. OsiguroMi d.o.o. je insurtech kompanija iz Novog Sada, osnovana 2019. godine sa jednom idejom: da osiguranje prestane da bude papirologija i postane tihi servis ugrađen u alate koje ljudi već koriste. Umesto da korisnik kupuje polisu na posebnom sajtu, naša tehnologija se integriše direktno u aplikacije za rezervaciju putovanja, agro-platforme i prodajne sisteme organizatora festivala — i polisa nastaje u trenutku transakcije. Radimo sa B2B partnerima širom Srbije i EU: putničkim platformama, zadrugama, organizatorima open-air događaja. Naš tim od 58 zaposlenih dolazi iz osiguranja, softverskog inženjerstva i analize podataka. Osnivači Milena Čabarkapa i Dragan Horvat prethodno su radili u reosiguranju i fintech sektoru, što je oblikovalo naš pristup: prvo model, pa produkt. Ono što nas razlikuje nije marketing — razlikuje nas API koji se može uključiti za manje od jednog radnog dana i parametarski okidači koji ne zahtevaju korisnikov zahtev za naknadu. Isplata se dešava automatski ili ne, na osnovu merljivih podataka: kašnjenje leta, količina padavina, otkazivanje događaja. Nema formulara, nema čekanja. Klijenti naših partnera to retko primete dok im ne zatreba, a onda primete odmah.
2. Pokušali smo da korigujemo prag na osnovu istorijskih razlika između stanica i terena, ali to je gruba aproksimacija. Imamo pristup RHMZS podacima i podacima tri privatne agrometeo mreže, ukupno oko 140 tačaka merenja u regionu. Razmišljali smo o satelitskim indeksima vlažnosti tla, ali nismo sigurni kako pouzdano spojiti te izvore u jedan okidač. Cilj je da do sledeće sezone ispravljamo isplate na osnovu prostorno tačnijih procena padavina po parceli, bez potpune zamene ugovornog praga.

Ova integracija je prva u agro-sektoru za OsiguroMi i označava ulazak kompanije na tržište koje do sada nije pokrila. {"company":{"id":"C001","name":"ArmaturaSec d.o.o.","sector":"Cybersecurity","employees":67,"founded":2008,"location":"Zrenjanin","language":"en","about":"ArmaturaSec d.o.o. has been building network security hardware in Zrenjanin since 2008. We started by selling simple firewall appliances to regional electricity distributors who needed to segment their control networks from corporate IT. Over fifteen years that focus narrowed: today every product we ship is designed specifically for operational technology environments — the kind of networks that run pumps, switchgear, and assembly lines, not office computers. Our customers are energy utilities, water treatment operators, and discrete manufacturers in Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. They are not looking for cloud dashboards or vendor lock-in; they need a device that sits in a metal cabinet at a substation or pump station, runs for years without attention, and tells someone when something is wrong. data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We process around 9,000 flight-delay compensation claims per month, fully automatically, without human review. The internal audit for Q3 2023 showed that 3.1% of payouts were triggered by data errors from the flight-status data provider — incorrect timestamps, duplicate entries, flights that were technically cancelled but displayed as delayed. That is not a negligible percentage when we are talking about payouts in euros. We currently work with a single external flight-status API. We attempted to introduce simple anomaly-detection rules, but false alarms block legitimate payouts. We need a method that can assess the credibility of incoming data before the trigger activates a payout — preferably in real time, because the whole point of the product is that the user receives a notification before leaving the airport. We have a log of all previous API calls and payouts, which amounts to around 340,000 entries in total. The budget for this is not unlimited — we are looking for a solution that can operate within our existing infrastructure, not a new system built from scratch."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We signed a distribution agreement with the Vienna-based travel booking platform ViennaJourney GmbH and were supposed to start selling in the first quarter of 2024. However, the process of obtaining a licence from the Austrian regulator FMA has been stalled for seven months. Our legal representative who was handling the case submitted their resignation last summer and the documentation was left incomplete. We found a new adviser, but the procedure is starting practically from scratch because FMA requires certain documents certified by the person who originally submitted the application. This is a regulatory, not a technical, problem — but it has a direct impact on revenue because ViennaJourney GmbH has included our product in its plan for the summer season. We are not looking for shortcuts; we are looking for someone who knows the FMA procedure from the inside and who can help us put the documentation together in a way that will not be sent back for a third time. Time pressure exists: if we do not obtain the licence by May 2024, the partner will push the integration back by an entire season."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"We are developing parametric insurance for open-air festival organisers: the policy is triggered if the precipitation forecast exceeds a threshold on event days, or if the authorities prohibit the event from taking place due to weather conditions. To set the price, we need stable loss curves. Our database contains just under 200 historical festival events in the region with accompanying weather data — that is too few for classical actuarial methods, the curves are unstable and the margins we need to charge become uncompetitive. We tried to supplement the database with data from open sources and news archives, but the quality and consistency are uneven. We are considering making broader use of meteorological data — for example, extreme-value statistics for each region and season — and building the model from the bottom up rather than purely from event history. We do not have the capacity to carry this through to completion on our own, as our actuarial team numbers two people. Concrete goal: a pricing methodology that yields reasonable confidence intervals even with a small set of historical events, applicable to different locations in the region."}]}

The policy is linked to the user's cadastral parcel and tracks precipitation based on available meteorological data for the corresponding microzone. The director of the Polje.rs platform, Aleksandar Mišković, stated: 'Our users have been asking for years for a solution that works without bureaucracy. This is concrete and measurable.' According to internal data from the OsiguroMi team, approximately 1,200 policies were activated in the first 30 days since launch. The trigger season for winter wheat begins in April 2024. This integration is the first in the agro-sector for OsiguroMi and marks the company's entry into a market it has not previously covered. The next step is calibration of the model based on feedback arriving from farms during the pilot period."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"Our agro-product pays out a benefit when the official meteorological station records a rainfall amount below the contracted threshold in a given period. The problem is that the nearest station is sometimes 30 kilometres from the plot — and across those 30 km there can be a mountain range, a river valley or an urban zone, all of which drastically alter local rainfall. We are receiving feedback from partners in Vojvodina and Bačka that payouts reached them when the field had not even dried out, or that there were none when they had lost their crop. We tried to correct the threshold on the basis of historical differences between stations and terrain, but that is a rough approximation. We have access to RHMZS data and data from three private agrometeorological networks, totalling around 140 measurement points in the region. We have been considering satellite soil-moisture indices, but we are not certain how to reliably combine those sources into a single trigger. The aim is to correct payouts by the next season on the basis of spatially more accurate rainfall estimates per plot, without completely replacing the contracted threshold."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"OsiguroMi is an API-first platform for embedding parametric micro-insurance. Our partners are platforms, applications and B2B services that want to offer insurance as part of their product — without needing to become an insurer themselves. How it works: a partner integrates our API into their checkout or booking page. When a user completes a reservation, our system automatically generates a policy based on the transaction parameters — destination, date, value, plot location and similar. The policy is sent to the user within a few seconds. If a trigger occurs — a flight is delayed beyond a defined threshold, rainfall falls below the contracted limit, an event is cancelled — payment is initiated without any claim on the part of the user. Our B2B partners today include the travel agency MontFlite from Belgrade, the agro-platform Polje.rs and the festival organiser SoundRavine Events. Through their channels, our policies are active with more than 40,000 end users. Technical characteristics of our integration:"},{"line":2,"english":"— Sandbox environment for testing without real data"},{"line":3,"english":"— Webhooks for real-time notifications"},{"line":4,"english":"— SLA of 99.7% availability We support integrations within one business day for standard use cases. For non-standard triggers or new market segments, we work through a pilot programme lasting four to six weeks. We are not a broker or intermediary in the classical sense — we are the technological and actuarial layer that sits between the reinsurer and digital distribution channels. Each of our products is covered by a contract with a reinsurer before it goes to market."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"When we completed the internal payout audit for the third quarter in October 2023, the number that stood out was 3.1%. That is how many of our automatic flight delay payouts should not have been triggered — not due to a policy error, not due to customer fraud, but due to bad data that entered the system before the trigger had even checked anything. Our claims processing mechanism works fast because it has to. A customer delayed on a flight needs a notification while they are still at the airport. That means the system makes a decision in under 60 seconds from the moment the flight status API reports a change. The problem is that this API sometimes reports changes that are artefacts of the system, not reality — duplicate entries, a flight reclassified from 'cancelled' to 'delayed' for operator technical reasons, timestamps that do not correspond to the actual gate status. In absolute numbers, 3.1% of 9,000 monthly claims means approximately 279 incorrect payouts per month. Each payout in this category amounts to between 15 and 60 EUR. It is not a disaster, but it is a systematic drain that accumulates. What we did not have is a filter that would check the consistency of incoming data before the trigger. We are now looking for exactly that: not a system that slows down processing, but a validation layer that can identify implausible combinations of data and either send them for a short manual review or hold them for 90 seconds until confirmation arrives from an alternative source. If you work on problems like these or have experience with anomaly detection in real-time API streams, we are open to a conversation."}]}

Review the claims of need C005-CH1.
It is about: company Kardiolink a.d. (C005), challenge C005-CH1.

Claims:
1. The KL-Patch 72 consumes 18 mAh per day when Bluetooth is active and runs on a 54 mAh lithium cell; active patients who trigger frequent syncs risk battery depletion before the 72-hour wear period ends. The company needs to reduce active current draw by at least 35% while maintaining 250 Hz sampling rate and has instrumented reference hardware with a Keysight N6705C power analyzer available for measurement. [C005-CH1, C005]
2. Kardiolink has twelve people working across hardware, firmware, and algorithm development with a shared lab equipped for electronics prototyping, signal acquisition testing, and device-level EMC pre-compliance testing. [C005]
3. The company has instrumented reference hardware in the lab with a Keysight N6705C power analyzer and can provide full current profiles. [C005-CH1]
4. Kardiolink runs FreeRTOS on an ARM Cortex-M4 with a Nordic Semiconductor nRF52840 handling ECG acquisition at 250 Hz and BLE communication. [C005, C005/job/2024-02-05/Embedded Firmware Engineer — Low-Power BLE Systems]
5. Sampling rate cannot drop below 250 Hz or the clinical validity of the signal is affected. [C005-CH1]
6. The company has already tuned BLE advertising intervals, moved to BLE 5.0 long-range PHY for some use cases, and switched to a lower-power MCU variant, and is now within a few milliamps of what firmware changes alone can achieve. [C005-CH1]

Subjects covered include mathematics, Serbian language, Hungarian language, and basic natural sciences for ages six to twelve. claim.text: Suncokret Eko has spent nearly a year preparing an application for the European Biochar Certificate scheme to register carbon removal credits, but has not yet submitted a complete application. The scheme requires chain-of-custody records, feedstock declarations, specific lab analyses, and a written quality management description aligned to the framework document, which is updated periodically. Our biochar product tests at around 55% fixed carbon but customers in Germany need at least 70% for soil-amendment certification; we've tried raising pyrolysis temperature but that cuts yield by nearly a third and makes the economics fall apart.

Our biochar consistently comes out with around 55% fixed carbon when we run the pyrolyser at 500–520 °C, which is where our yield is commercially acceptable. Buyers in Germany and the Netherlands need at least 70% fixed carbon to qualify under soil-amendment certification schemes. We have pushed the temperature up to 650 °C and beyond in trials, and we do hit the 70% threshold, but the mass yield drops from roughly 28% to under 20%, which means we need about 40% more raw material to fill the same order. At current feedstock and energy costs that wipes out the price premium we get for certified biochar. We have also tried extending the hold time at lower temperatures rather than raising the peak, but the gains in fixed carbon are modest. We have two years of batch logs covering temperature profiles, feedstock moisture, particle size and output quality that we can share. Our PLC programs for different customers are each a custom spaghetti of ladder logic; when we want to push a safety patch we have to touch 38 separate codebases and it takes three engineers two full weeks.

Over the years we have written a separate PLC program for almost every customer installation. Each one started from a rough template and then grew as the customer asked for changes during commissioning and after. Today we have 38 active codebases across our installed base, all written in ladder logic in TIA Portal, and they have drifted apart to the point where a safety-related patch — for example, an emergency stop sequence change required by a new machinery directive interpretation — has to be found, adapted, and tested in every single one of them. The last time we did this it took three of our engineers two full weeks, and they still found two sites where the logic was different enough that the standard fix did not apply cleanly. We know the answer is some form of modular library or structured code reuse, but every time we try to start, the daily project load pulls the engineers away. We have one senior PLC programmer, Dragan Ilić, who understands the full picture, but he is also our lead on active commissioning projects. Our quality assurance team writes regression tests by hand for every firmware release; with four hardware variants and monthly release cycles that's eating about 35% of total engineering time and we're still shipping bugs that automated tests should catch.

We release firmware roughly once a month across four hardware variants: the original NetGuard-OT board, the Mini, and two older boards we still maintain for clients under long-term support contracts. Before each release our QA team runs a regression suite that they have been building by hand since 2015. The suite now has around 1,400 test cases. Writing new cases for a feature, updating old ones when hardware behaviour changes, and running everything on four boards takes about two and a half weeks of engineering time per cycle. That is the 35% figure. We have also shipped three bugs in the past year that the regression suite should have caught but did not because the relevant test cases were out of date. We have tried generating tests from our internal protocol specifications but the tooling we built for that was brittle and the team abandoned it. Review the claims of profile R0127.
It is about: researcher Emilija Tešić (R0127).

Claims:
1. Hallucination detection in long-form language model outputs using atomic claim decomposition and natural language inference. [SYN-PUB-01679]
2. Citation verification and grounding for retrieval-augmented generation systems, linking generated claims to source passages. [SYN-PUB-01682, SYN-PUB-01678]
3. Explanation fidelity evaluation in instruction-tuned language models, comparing self-explanations to saliency and perturbation-based methods. [SYN-PUB-01683]
4. Post-hoc explanation methods including LIME, SHAP, and integrated gradients, with analysis of their consistency under distribution shift. [SYN-PUB-01681]
5. Retrieval quality effects on faithfulness in RAG systems, measured through controlled experiments with varied retrieval precision. [SYN-PUB-01680]
6. Factual consistency checking in generated text using natural language inference as a proxy. [SYN-PUB-01675]
7. Uncertainty quantification in transformer-based question answering using Monte Carlo dropout. [SYN-PUB-01677]
8. Knowledge encoding in pre-trained language models across layers using probing classifiers. [SYN-PUB-01676]
9. Open to joint projects with companies developing document automation or compliance tools, contract research on hallucination detection and citation verification for RAG systems, and industrial PhD supervision. [R0127]
10. Collaborated with a regional legal information provider during the VERIFAI-RS project, advising on requirements and evaluating a prototype verification module against real workflows. [SYN-PRJ-0556]
11. Open to consulting on evaluation methodology for AI-generated text quality and student internships related to annotation tool development and benchmark construction. [R0127]
12. Has provided informal consulting to software companies in Novi Sad on explainability reporting requirements under EU AI regulations. [R0127]

Review the claims of pair C005-CH2:R0057.
It is about: researcher Lazar Šarić (R0057) and company Kardiolink a.d. (C005), challenge C005-CH2.

Claims:
1. Kardiolink's core difficulty is a lossless compression algorithm tailored to ECG signal structure that exceeds the current 3:1 ratio; lossy compression is blocked because the regulatory submission is built around lossless compression. [C005-CH2]
2. Šarić's work covers lossless and near-lossless compression of physiological time series using discrete cosine transform and wavelet transforms, including rate-distortion analysis and codec design for medical signals. [SYN-PUB-00762, SYN-PUB-00760, SYN-PUB-00755]
3. Šarić has published on beat-aligned signal framing and adaptive parameter tuning for physiological signal compression, which directly addresses ECG's quasi-periodic structure. [SYN-PUB-00755, SYN-PUB-00757]
4. Šarić has published on learned compression models with small recurrent networks and entropy coding for ECG signals. [SYN-PUB-00763, SYN-PUB-00761]
5. Šarić and Kardiolink would design and benchmark a lossless ECG compression codec that exploits beat-aligned framing and entropy coding on Kardiolink's 140,000-segment labelled dataset, targeting a compression ratio beyond 3:1 on 16-bit, 250 Hz, 3-channel data from the KL-Patch 72, while remaining strictly lossless as required by the regulatory submission. [C005-CH2, SYN-PUB-00755, SYN-PUB-00757, SYN-PUB-00763, SYN-PUB-00761, SYN-PUB-00762, SYN-PUB-00760]
6. The expertise record covers lossless and near-lossless compression; whether the methods operate in a strictly lossless mode without any approximation step is not confirmed by the cited publications. [SYN-PUB-00762, SYN-PUB-00760, SYN-PUB-00755]

Sources:

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"The study analyses how different levels of disagreement between annotators affect the performance of classification models in the Serbian legal domain. The experiment uses three differently annotated versions of the same corpus of 3,600 documents: the first annotated by legal experts (high consistency, kappa = 0.82), the second by law students (medium consistency, kappa = 0.67), and the third by general users via a platform similar to the crowdsourcing model (low consistency, kappa = 0.54). Logistic regression, Random Forest, and a BERT-based model were trained on each version. The results show that the difference in the F1 measure between expert and crowdsourced annotation ranges between 3.1 and 7.8 percentage points, depending on the model and legal category. The BERT model demonstrates greater robustness to noisy labels than classical models. The implications for the practical organisation of annotation projects in the legal domain are discussed."}]}

data.text: {"lines":[{"line":1,"english":"The paper presents a system for the automatic classification of court decisions of the Supreme Court of Cassation of the Republic of Serbia into 12 legal areas. The corpus consists of 4,200 anonymised decisions collected between 2003 and 2008. An SVM classifier with a linear kernel was applied to TF-IDF vectorised texts, with experimentation involving different n-gram sizes (unigrams, bigrams and trigrams). Evaluation was carried out using fivefold cross-validation. The best result was achieved with a combination of unigrams and bigrams: the macro F1 score was 0.81. The error analysis shows that categories with a small number of examples and ambiguous terminology (e.g. labour law versus commercial law) are the most difficult to distinguish. The paper also describes the annotation procedure and the inter-annotator agreement metric (Cohen's kappa = 0.79)."}]}

It is about: researcher Lazar Šarić (R0057).

Compression of Multi-Lead ECG Using Joint Sparsity Across Leads (2020, journal, Journal of Biomedical Signal Analysis).
Authors: Lazar Šarić (R0057); Jelena Graovac (outside co-author); Sorin Moldovan (outside co-author).
Keywords: 12-lead ECG; joint sparsity; multi-lead compression; dictionary learning.
(no abstract)

[SYN-PUB-00758] publication · Sparse Coding of PPG Signals Using a Learned Overcomplete Dictionary · 2019 · researchers R0057
Sparse Coding of PPG Signals Using a Learned Overcomplete Dictionary (2019, conference, Biomedical Compression and Coding Workshop (BCCW), Ljubljana).
Authors: Lazar Šarić (R0057); Marek Kowalski (outside co-author); Milena Vuković (outside co-author).
Keywords: PPG; sparse coding; K-SVD; overcomplete dictionary; matching pursuit.
Photoplethysmography (PPG) signals share quasi-periodic pulse structure but exhibit waveform variation due to respiratory modulation and motion artefact. This work trains a 256-atom overcomplete dictionary on a 10,000-pulse corpus using the K-SVD algorithm, then encodes each 200-sample pulse segment as a sparse combination of at most eight atoms, with atom indices and coefficients quantised to 8 and 16 bits respectively. A greedy matching pursuit selects atoms sequentially. On a held-out test set of 3,200 pulses from 16 subjects collected with a finger oximeter at 100 Hz, the method achieves a mean reconstruction error of 0.6% PRD at 3.2 bits per sample, compared to 4.1 bits per sample for a 12-coefficient per-pulse DCT coder at the same PRD. Keywords: transfer learning; domain adaptation; labour law; intermediate pretraining; Croatian Serbian.
Transformer-based language models pretrained on large general corpora require substantial fine-tuning data to adapt to specialised legal domains. This paper examines whether intermediate pretraining on a moderately sized Croatian–Serbian legal text collection (approximately 120,000 sentences from publicly accessible legislation and court decisions) improves downstream performance on a Serbian labour-law classification task with only 640 training examples. Four model variants are compared: multilingual BERT with no intermediate pretraining, the same model with intermediate pretraining on the combined corpus, and two models pretrained on each national subset separately. Intermediate pretraining on the combined corpus achieves the best macro F1 (0.72) on a held-out test set of 160 examples, surpassing the no-pretraining baseline by 0.11. Differences between the Croatian-only and Serbian-only intermediate pretraining conditions are modest, suggesting that vocabulary overlap rather than syntactic similarity drives the gain. [SYN-PUB-00215] publication · Delta-of-Delta Encoding for Monotonic Sensor Counters in Relational Column Stores · 2013 · researchers R0019
Delta-of-Delta Encoding for Monotonic Sensor Counters in Relational Column Stores (2013, journal, Novi Sad Journal of Computing and Information Science).
Authors: Petar Hadžić (R0019); Miroslav Topalović (outside co-author).
Keywords: delta encoding; monotonic counters; columnar storage; compression ratio.
Monotonic counter sequences produced by industrial pulse sensors exhibit strong first-order and second-order differences that standard LZ-family compressors exploit poorly when applied at the row level. This paper evaluates a purely arithmetic delta-of-delta scheme applied within a columnar storage engine on sequences of 32-bit unsigned integers sampled at 1 kHz. Experiments use 14 days of vibration counter data from a water-treatment facility logging 48 sensor channels, yielding roughly 58 billion raw values. The scheme is compared against Snappy, LZ4, and a Gorilla-style float codec adapted for integers. Delta-of-delta achieves a compression ratio of 18.3:1 against raw binary, outperforming LZ4 (11.1:1) with 40 % lower decompression CPU time. Encoding throughput on a single core reaches 920 MB/s. The paper also derives a closed-form bound on the representable range for a fixed bit-width delta register and proposes a lightweight overflow-detection branch that adds under 2 % latency overhead.

Law firm users copy our AI-generated research summaries directly into briefs without reading them, and twice this year the summaries contained an outdated precedent; we need a way to attach confidence scores and source provenance to every generated sentence.

We generate paragraph-level summaries of relevant court decisions and legal arguments. Several law firm users have told us they paste these summaries directly into draft briefs without checking the source. Twice this year a summary referenced a precedent that had been overturned or amended, and in one case a firm submitted a brief containing the outdated citation before catching the error. We take this seriously. What we want to build is a system that attaches a confidence score and a direct source link to every sentence or claim in a generated summary, so a lawyer can see at a glance whether a statement is based on one decision or fifty, and how recent the most recent supporting case is. Emilija Tešić (R0127): Full Professor, Department of Mathematics and Informatics, Faculty of Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Artificial Intelligence; Natural Language Processing; Machine Learning; Knowledge Representation and Reasoning.
Keywords: explainable AI; hallucination detection; large language models; retrieval-augmented generation; citation grounding; fact verification; faithfulness evaluation; saliency methods; natural language inference; benchmark construction.
Bio: Emilija Tešić received her BSc and MSc degrees in Mathematics and Computer Science from the University of Novi Sad in 2001 and 2004, respectively, and completed her PhD at the same institution in 2009 with a dissertation on formal verification methods for inference systems. She joined the Department of Mathematics and Informatics as an assistant professor in 2010 and was promoted to full professor in 2020. Her research group focuses on explainability frameworks for machine learning models, automated detection of factual inconsistencies in large language model outputs, and grounding mechanisms that link generated text to verifiable source documents in retrieval-augmented generation pipelines. She teaches courses in logic programming, knowledge representation, and applied machine learning. Review the claims of profile R0484.
It is about: researcher Jovan Puzović (R0484).

Claims:
1. Field extraction from inspection certificates using conditional random fields with spatial context features derived from token bounding boxes. [SYN-PUB-05474]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-05474] publication · Combining CRF Sequence Labelling with Spatial Context Features for Field Extraction in Inspection Certificates · 2016 · researchers R0460, R0484
Combining CRF Sequence Labelling with Spatial Context Features for Field Extraction in Inspection Certificates (2016, journal, Journal of Information Science and Engineering).
Authors: Tatjana Sremčević (outside co-author); Predrag Ljubojević (R0460); Nikola Grujičić (outside co-author); Jovan Puzović (R0484).
Keywords: conditional random fields; sequence labelling; field extraction; inspection certificates; spatial features.
Inspection certificates issued by accredited testing laboratories follow loose conventions but no single fixed template. This work treats field extraction as a sequence labelling problem over sorted text tokens, augmented with spatial features derived from each token's bounding box and its nearest neighbours. A conditional random field model is trained on 1,100 annotated inspection certificates and evaluated on a held-out set of 275 certificates from laboratories not represented in training. The feature set includes token geometry, font-size estimates from bounding-box height, relative page position, left-margin alignment, and the label of the spatially closest token. Adding spatial context features raised per-field extraction accuracy from 72.3 % to 83.7 % compared with a purely sequential baseline. Error analysis identified measurement units as the most frequently mislabelled token class. The trained model is integrated into a prototype pipeline, and processing throughput of 8.4 certificates per second is reported on a standard 2014-era server.

Review the claims of profile R0019.
It is about: researcher Petar Hadžić (R0019).

Claims:
1. Delta-of-delta and adaptive bit-packing encoding for time-series, with SIMD acceleration for bit-packing decompression. [SYN-PUB-00215, SYN-PUB-00219]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-00215] publication · Delta-of-Delta Encoding for Monotonic Sensor Counters in Relational Column Stores · 2013 · researchers R0019
Delta-of-Delta Encoding for Monotonic Sensor Counters in Relational Column Stores (2013, journal, Novi Sad Journal of Computing and Information Science).
Authors: Petar Hadžić (R0019); Miroslav Topalović (outside co-author).
Keywords: delta encoding; monotonic counters; columnar storage; compression ratio.
Monotonic counter sequences produced by industrial pulse sensors exhibit strong first-order and second-order differences that standard LZ-family compressors exploit poorly when applied at the row level. This paper evaluates a purely arithmetic delta-of-delta scheme applied within a columnar storage engine on sequences of 32-bit unsigned integers sampled at 1 kHz. Experiments use 14 days of vibration counter data from a water-treatment facility logging 48 sensor channels, yielding roughly 58 billion raw values. The scheme is compared against Snappy, LZ4, and a Gorilla-style float codec adapted for integers. Delta-of-delta achieves a compression ratio of 18.3:1 against raw binary, outperforming LZ4 (11.1:1) with 40 % lower decompression CPU time. Encoding throughput on a single core reaches 920 MB/s. The paper also derives a closed-form bound on the representable range for a fixed bit-width delta register and proposes a lightweight overflow-detection branch that adds under 2 % latency overhead.

This paper proposes a method for automatic detection of such inconsistencies at the sentence level, using a classifier that takes as features the distribution of script blocks, bigram frequencies, and morphosyntactic signals. The pilot companies had collections of between 8,000 and 45,000 documents. We measured search precision before and after the introduction of normalization, user response, and implementation costs. data.message:
Review the claims of profile R0741.
It is about: researcher Snežana Todorović (R0741).

Claims:
1. Led as work package leader an Interreg project designing federated index infrastructure for cross-lingual document discovery, piloted with two municipal archives. [SYN-PRJ-0559]

Sources:
[SYN-PRJ-0559] project · Cross-Lingual Document Discovery in Regional Public Administration Archives · 2023 · researchers R0741
CROSSDOC: Cross-Lingual Document Discovery in Regional Public Administration Archives (Interreg IPA Hungary–Serbia, 2023–2026).
Participants: R0741 work package leader.
Partners: Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad; University of Debrecen, Faculty of Informatics, Hungary; City Archive of Subotica; Municipal Document Centre of Pécs, Hungary.
CROSSDOC aims to improve access to administrative documents held by Hungarian and Serbian public bodies by building a shared cross-lingual retrieval layer. The Serbian technical team, led by Todorović, is responsible for the index infrastructure work package, including the design of a federated index architecture that allows each national partner to retain custody of its documents while exposing a unified query interface. The system will be piloted with two municipal archives containing approximately 400,000 documents each. Hungarian-language tokenisation and transliteration components are contributed by the University of Debrecen partner.

1. Uticaj morfološke redukcije na preciznost pretrage srpskih višeskriptnih dokumenata (2013, journal, Infoteka: Časopis za informatiku i bibliotekarstvo).

In this paper we examine how stemming and lemmatisation interact with the script normalisation procedure in the construction of a search index. We use three stemmers available for the Serbian language — two rule-based and one statistical — and combine them with a phonemic canonicalisation step described in previous papers. The evaluation was carried out on a subset of the CLEF 2012 collection containing documents in both scripts. The results show that the order of operations (stemming before or after script normalisation) affects recall, whereby stemming after normalisation consistently yields better results for all three combinations (an improvement of 4 to 9 percentage points in MAP). Phoneme-Based Token Canonicalization for Serbian Script Unification (2011, journal, Journal of Language Technology and Computational Linguistics).
Authors: Stefan Dragić (R0349); Milena Kovačević (outside co-author); Radovan Ostojić (outside co-author).
Keywords: phoneme canonicalization; Serbian; script unification; legal text retrieval.
Serbian is officially written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts, and documents frequently contain tokens in both scripts within a single sentence or paragraph. This paper presents a token canonicalization procedure in which each token is mapped to a phoneme sequence using deterministic grapheme-to-phoneme rules derived from Serbian orthographic conventions, and the resulting phoneme string serves as the canonical form for retrieval purposes. We evaluated the approach on a manually annotated gold standard of 4 200 query–document relevance pairs drawn from a legal corpus of 38 000 court decisions. data.message:
Review the claims of pair C007-CH2:R0992.
It is about: researcher Đorđe Vukelić (R0992) and company Suncokret Eko d.o.o. (C007), challenge C007-CH2.

Claims:
1. Suncokret Eko has collected most required lab data and roughly 18 months of production records but lacks capacity to identify remaining documentation gaps and write the quality management section in technical English for auditors (C007-CH2). [C007-CH2]
2. Vukelić has co-authored publications on biochar characterisation evaluated against European Biochar Certificate criteria (SYN-PUB-10355, SYN-PUB-10349, SYN-PUB-10348). [SYN-PUB-10355, SYN-PUB-10349, SYN-PUB-10348]
3. Vukelić holds a granted patent on a process for producing certified-grade biochar from sunflower husk aligned to EBC requirements (SYN-PAT-033). [SYN-PAT-033]
4. Vukelić is open to consulting on biochar quality assurance and contract research with industry partners (R0992). [R0992]
5. Vukelić and Suncokret Eko would work together to map the company's existing lab data and production records against European Biochar Certificate criteria, identify remaining documentation gaps, and write the quality management section of the EBC application in technically accurate English suitable for auditors (C007-CH2, SYN-PUB-10355, SYN-PUB-10349, SYN-PAT-033). [C007-CH2, SYN-PUB-10355, SYN-PUB-10349, SYN-PAT-033]
6. Vukelić is currently committed at roughly 0.8 FTE research capacity due to PYROLINK obligations and a full teaching load, which may make availability tight against the end-of-year submission deadline (R0992). [R0992]
7. The records cover biochar characterisation and EBC criteria evaluation; they do not cover writing chain-of-custody documentation or quality management narratives for EBC auditors specifically. [SYN-PUB-10355, SYN-PUB-10349, SYN-PAT-033]
8. The 4,000 EUR budget is the only budget stated for this work, and the EBC framework is updated periodically, which may require additional revision effort within that budget (C007-CH2). [C007-CH2]

claim.text: The company's core difficulty is the temperature–yield trade-off in a batch slow-pyrolysis reactor that it cannot resolve with existing knowledge, and the constraint is no new capital equipment within six months (C007-CH1).

rejected.reason: C007-CH1 describes the fixed-carbon vs. yield trade-off in pyrolysis and states 'We need a way to improve fixed-carbon content without either wrecking yield or requiring capital we do not have for a new reactor' and a 'process adjustment we can test on our existing equipment within six months,' but does not mention a 'batch slow-pyrolysis reactor' specifically — it says 'pyrolyser' and 'existing equipment'; the claim's characterisation of 'batch slow-pyrolysis reactor' is not stated in the text, and 'core difficulty' framing and 'existing knowledge' constraint are not verbatim but the substance (trade-off, no capital, six months) is present.

claim.text: Vukelić co-authored publications on temperature and residence-time optimisation for biochar yield and structural properties via response-surface design and fixed-bed reactor experiments (SYN-PUB-10356, SYN-PUB-05935, SYN-PUB-05944).

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-10356 covers temperature–residence-time response-surface design for biochar yield and fixed carbon in a fixed-bed reactor; SYN-PUB-05944 covers residence-time effects on fixed-bed pyrolysis; but SYN-PUB-05935 is about corona-discharge optimisation for packaging boards — it uses response-surface methodology but has nothing to do with biochar yield, structural properties, or reactor experiments, so the claim that it covers 'temperature and residence-time optimisation for biochar yield and structural properties' is not supported by that source.

claim.text: Vukelić co-authored work on pyrolysis kinetics of agricultural residues including sunflower husks, and on thermogravimetric analysis of particle size effects on pyrolysis kinetics (SYN-PUB-10346, SYN-PUB-10351).

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-10346 covers TGA pyrolysis kinetics of sunflower husks (an agricultural residue) by Vukelić, and SYN-PUB-10351 covers particle size effects on pyrolysis kinetics via TGA for wheat straw — not sunflower husks — so the claim that SYN-PUB-10351 is about 'particle size effects on pyrolysis kinetics' of 'agricultural residues' is broadly correct, but the claim bundles both under 'pyrolysis kinetics of agricultural residues including sunflower husks,' which is only stated in SYN-PUB-10346; SYN-PUB-10351 uses wheat straw, not sunflower husks, so the grouping implies both cover sunflower husks, which is not supported.

rejected.reason: This is a proposal claim; checking whether the company's need and all stated facts about each side are in the cited text: C007-CH1 confirms the two-year batch logs, existing reactor, six-month window, and ≥70% fixed carbon target; SYN-PUB-10356 and SYN-PUB-05935 and SYN-PAT-033 support response-surface methods and EBC criteria; however, 'maize cob feedstocks' are not mentioned in any cited source (C007-CH1 only mentions feedstock generically; the patent and publications cover corn stover, sunflower husk, wheat straw — not maize cobs specifically), and 'particle size' as a varied factor is not mentioned in C007-CH1's description of what needs to be tested, making 'maize cob' an unsupported addition.

claim.text: The published record covers sunflower husks; maize cobs as a co-feedstock are not mentioned in the cited works, so the optimised process window may need extension to cover that feedstock (SYN-PUB-10346, SYN-PUB-10348, SYN-PUB-10354).

rejected.reason: SYN-PUB-10346 covers sunflower husks; SYN-PUB-10348 covers wheat straw and lignite co-pyrolysis; SYN-PUB-10354 covers sunflower husks (torrefaction pre-treatment); none of these cited works mention maize cobs, so the claim that maize cobs are not mentioned is consistent, but the claim adds a judgement about what 'the optimised process window may need,' which is an editorial inference not found in any cited text.

claim.text: The patent covers temperature–residence-time feedback control; the company's constraint forbids capital investment in a new reactor, so any feedback-control hardware implied by the patent would need to be ruled out or substituted by manual protocol adjustments (C007-CH1, SYN-PAT-033).

It is about: researcher Snežana Todorović (R0741) and company PravniPilot a.d. (C006), challenge C006-CH4.

Claims:
1. Todorović co-authored work on hybrid sparse-dense retrieval architectures evaluated on Serbian and multilingual news corpora (SYN-PUB-08207), and co-authored work on learned sparse retrieval models fine-tuned for Serbian, Croatian and Bosnian text (SYN-PUB-08208). [SYN-PUB-08207, SYN-PUB-08208]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-08207] publication · Hybrid Sparse–Dense Retrieval: Combining BM25 and Vector Indexes Without Score Normalisation Heuristics · 2021 · researchers R0741
Hybrid Sparse–Dense Retrieval: Combining BM25 and Vector Indexes Without Score Normalisation Heuristics (2021, journal, Journal of Information Retrieval Research (JIRR)).
Authors: Snežana Todorović (R0741); Rade Milošević (outside co-author); Marco Dellarocca (outside co-author); Ana Kovačević (outside co-author).
Keywords: hybrid retrieval; BM25; dense retrieval; reciprocal rank fusion; multilingual.
Combining a lexical BM25 index with a dense vector index requires merging scores from incompatible distributions. Most practical systems rely on hand-tuned linear interpolation weights or min–max normalisation, both of which are sensitive to corpus and query distribution shifts. We propose a rank-based fusion approach grounded in reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) that requires no score normalisation and is calibrated using a small set of 500 labelled query–document pairs. Evaluation on two corpora—a 3-million-document Serbian legal archive and a 7-million-document multilingual news collection—shows that the proposed method matches or exceeds the best normalisation baseline on NDCG@10 (gains of 1.8 and 2.4 points respectively) while being robust to out-of-distribution query sets. Latency overhead compared to BM25 alone is 22 ms at the 95th percentile on the larger corpus when vector retrieval runs on GPU.

Authors: Vesna Ilić (outside co-author); Sanja Lukić (R0504); Lidija Radić (R0151); Marija Petrović (outside co-author).
Keywords: aceclofenac; co-crystal; twin-screw extrusion; solubility; stability.
Aceclofenac is a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug with low aqueous solubility (0.011 mg mL⁻¹ at 25 °C). Twenty-two co-formers listed on the GRAS list were screened by LAG; five yielded new crystalline phases by PXRD. The three most stable candidates—nicotinamide, caffeine, and theophylline—were selected for full characterisation. DSC, TGA, PXRD, and Raman mapping confirmed co-crystal identity and purity. Aqueous solubility measured by the miniaturised shake-flask method (n = 3) increased to 0.034, 0.029, and 0.021 mg mL⁻¹ respectively for the three co-crystals. Phoneme-Based Token Canonicalization for Serbian Script Unification (2011, journal, Journal of Language Technology and Computational Linguistics).
Authors: Stefan Dragić (R0349); Milena Kovačević (outside co-author); Radovan Ostojić (outside co-author).
Keywords: phoneme canonicalization; Serbian; script unification; legal text retrieval.
Serbian is officially written in both Cyrillic and Latin scripts, and documents frequently contain tokens in both scripts within a single sentence or paragraph. This paper presents a token canonicalization procedure in which each token is mapped to a phoneme sequence using deterministic grapheme-to-phoneme rules derived from Serbian orthographic conventions, and the resulting phoneme string serves as the canonical form for retrieval purposes. We evaluated the approach on a manually annotated gold standard of 4 200 query–document relevance pairs drawn from a legal corpus of 38 000 court decisions. The phoneme-based canonical form reduced the out-of-vocabulary rate from 9.3% to 2.1% compared with a Latin-only baseline and from 11.7% to 2.4% compared with a Cyrillic-only baseline. Precision at rank 10 improved by 8 percentage points over both baselines. Edge cases involving foreign loanwords and proper nouns are discussed, and a set of override rules is proposed for the 230 most frequent exceptions identified in the corpus.

Co-crystal formation between furosemide and three pyridine derivatives: structural inference from PXRD and Raman spectroscopy in the absence of single-crystal data (2018, conference, Proceedings of the 6th Central European Symposium on Pharmaceutical Technology).
Authors: Marija Petrović (outside co-author); Vasilije Ivković (R0038); Vesna Ilić (outside co-author); Lidija Radić (R0151).
Keywords: furosemide; co-crystal; Raman spectroscopy; PXRD indexing; FaSSIF.
Three co-crystals of furosemide (a poorly soluble loop diuretic) with 2-aminopyridine, 3-hydroxypyridine, and 4,4′-bipyridine were prepared by LAG with acetonitrile and characterised entirely in polycrystalline form. Single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction could not be grown from any of the nine solvent systems attempted. Structural inference relied on indexing of PXRD patterns (DICVOL06 and TREOR90 algorithms), lattice parameter comparison with Cambridge Structural Database entries, and Raman band shifts. The carbonyl stretch of furosemide at 1678 cm⁻¹ shifted to 1663 cm⁻¹ in the 2-aminopyridine co-crystal, consistent with N–H···O hydrogen bonding. Review the claims of pair C007-CH2:R0992.
It is about: researcher Đorđe Vukelić (R0992) and company Suncokret Eko d.o.o. (C007), challenge C007-CH2.

Claims:
1. Vukelić has co-authored a publication on biochar characterisation evaluated against European Biochar Certificate criteria (SYN-PUB-10349). [SYN-PUB-10349]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-10349] publication · Characterisation of biochars from Vojvodina agricultural residues against European Biochar Certificate criteria · 2018 · researchers R0992
Characterisation of biochars from Vojvodina agricultural residues against European Biochar Certificate criteria (2018, journal, Agronomy and Soil Science Reports).
Authors: Đorđe Vukelić (R0992); Tamara Horvat (outside co-author); Ivana Rađenović (outside co-author); Lukas Brandt (outside co-author).
Keywords: biochar certification; EBC; PAH; heavy metals; Vojvodina.
Six biochar samples were produced from sunflower husks, wheat straw, and corn stover at 500 and 650 °C using identical slow pyrolysis conditions and subjected to full physicochemical characterisation aligned with European Biochar Certificate (EBC) version 9 criteria. Analyses included elemental composition (C, H, N, S, O), BET surface area, pore size distribution (Barrett–Joyner–Halenda method), pH and electrical conductivity in water extract, plant-available phosphorus, cation exchange capacity, and 16 EPA priority PAH congeners by GC-MS. All samples produced at 650 °C met EBC Basic grade for stable carbon (minimum 50% Corg). PAH totals ranged from 1.2 to 4.7 mg kg⁻¹ dry matter, below the EBC premium threshold of 6 mg kg⁻¹ for all samples. Heavy metal concentrations (Cd, Cr, Cu, Ni, Pb, Zn) remained well within limits. A scoring matrix comparing regional feedstocks is presented to guide commercial producers in Vojvodina.

Review the claims of proposal C006-CH1-R0484.
It is about: researcher Jovan Puzović (R0484) and company PravniPilot a.d. (C006), challenge C006-CH1.

Claims:
1. PravniPilot a.d. works in legal tech. [C006]
2. Jovan Puzović is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computing and Control Engineering, Faculty of Technical Sciences. [R0484]
3. A case-outcome prediction model trained on roughly 9,000 labelled Serbian commercial-dispute decisions achieves 61% accuracy, and the company estimates 40,000 clean labelled decisions are needed to reach accuracy worth advertising. [C006-CH1]
4. Basic data augmentation and fine-tuning of pre-trained multilingual models have not moved accuracy past 63% in internal tests. [C006-CH1]
5. Serbian courts do not publish decisions in a consistent machine-readable format, requiring significant cleaning before any decision can be used for training. [C006-CH1]
6. A 2023 study reports that multi-language transfer learning with extractive and abstractive techniques outperforms state-of-the-art extractive summarization on a low-resource legal corpus, setting a new baseline for abstractive summarization. [W4387008943]
7. A 2023 study reports that a translate-and-test pipeline separating translation from classification significantly improves cross-lingual text classification over competitive multilingual baselines on three benchmark datasets. [W4386902339]
8. A corpus of over two million published court decisions from Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, indexed in PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch, providing the source material for transfer learning. [C006]
9. Roughly 9,000 labelled commercial-dispute decisions and an internal annotation tool, with one full-time data engineer and two part-time annotators available for data quality and labelling. [C006, C006-CH1]
10. A development team that can allocate roughly two days per week to collaborative research, provided research output integrates directly into the production codebase. [C006]

The claims are checked one by one elsewhere: take them as given. In the proposal each one shows as ⟨claim N⟩.

the terms agreed up front.

Free text may propose new work and new data ("collect", "label", "set up", "measure", "aim for"), and may reason from the
claims. List a sentence only when it:
- presents as already true a fact about the company or the researcher (data, recordings, a dataset size, history,

- plans work that breaks a limit the company states (a rate it may not go below, hardware it cannot change).

Return an empty list when the free text is fine.

data.message:
Review the claims of pair C007-CH3:R0135.
It is about: researcher Veljko Savić (R0135) and company Suncokret Eko d.o.o. (C007), challenge C007-CH3.

Claims:
1. Suncokret Eko's pellet press breakdowns are caused by inconsistent moisture and particle-size properties from different suppliers, and the company needs a clearer picture of what incoming feedstock variance is acceptable (C007-CH3). [C007-CH3]
2. The researcher co-authored work on profilometry-based ring-die wear progression under variable moisture levels on a pelletisation line (SYN-PUB-01785). [SYN-PUB-01785]
3. The researcher co-authored a RUL estimation framework using a Bayesian degradation model integrated with NIR-based feedstock quality forecasting for pellet mill rollers (SYN-PUB-01794). [SYN-PUB-01794]
4. The researcher led the RELIODENSE project with Bioenergo d.o.o. as industry partner (SYN-PRJ-0334), and collaborated with Bioenergo d.o.o. including on-site instrumentation of their ring-die press (R0135). [SYN-PRJ-0334, R0135]

Sources:
[C007-CH3] challenge · Our pellet press breaks down about once a month because the sunflower husk feedstock has inconsistent moisture and particle size coming from different suppliers; downtime costs us roughly 15,000 EUR per incident when we have delivery commitments. · company C007
Our pellet press breaks down about once a month because the sunflower husk feedstock has inconsistent moisture and particle size coming from different suppliers; downtime costs us roughly 15,000 EUR per incident when we have delivery commitments.

Our pellet press line goes down roughly once a month. The root cause is almost always the same: sunflower husk material arriving with moisture content or particle size outside the range the press can handle. When moisture is above 14% the dies clog; when there is too much fine dust mixed with coarser pieces the compression is uneven and we get bearing failures. Wear mechanisms in multilayer TiAlN/TiN PVD coatings on carbide inserts: effect of bilayer period on performance in turning of austempered ductile iron (2022, journal, Wear).
Authors: Krzysztof Czyżewski (outside co-author); Petar Vranić (outside co-author); Miroslav Plančak (outside co-author); Filip Urošević (R0920).
Keywords: multilayer coating; TiAlN/TiN; bilayer period; ADI; crack propagation.
Multilayer TiAlN/TiN coatings with three bilayer periods—8 nm, 20 nm and 60 nm—were deposited by cathodic arc PVD on WC-6%Co inserts. Total coating thickness was maintained at 3.5 µm for all architectures. Turning of austempered ductile iron (ADI, Grade 800, 280 HB) was carried out at 180 m/min, feed 0.14 mm/rev, depth 1.2 mm, in dry conditions. Flank wear, notch wear and cutting force components (Fc, Ff, Fp) were monitored at 300 m intervals. Inserts with the 20 nm period showed 19 % lower flank wear rate than the 8 nm period and 34 % lower than the 60 nm period at 900 m cumulative distance. Nanoindentation hardness was highest for the 8 nm period (42 GPa) but this did not translate to the best wear performance. SEM of worn flanks revealed that the 20 nm architecture delayed crack propagation across interfaces more effectively. Cutting forces were within 8 % across all three architectures throughout testing.

Extending the standard knowledge-tracing model with slip and guess priors estimated from population response distributions (2014, journal, International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education).
Authors: Luka Đorđević (outside co-author); Nevena Simić (R0755); Anita Schulze (outside co-author); Bogdan Kapor (R0196); Emilija Zec (R0322).
Keywords: Bayesian knowledge tracing; slip and guess; EM algorithm; algebra tutoring.
The standard Bayesian knowledge-tracing (BKT) model assumes fixed, hand-tuned slip and guess parameters, which often leads to local optima and poor generalisation across learner populations. This paper proposes a population-informed BKT variant in which slip and guess priors are estimated from aggregate response distributions of a held-out calibration cohort before individual-level EM updating. The approach was tested on interaction logs from a secondary-school algebra tutoring system used by 2,104 students over one academic year, comprising 1.3 million item-response events. Compared to standard BKT, the population-prior model reduced mean absolute error in next-item predictions by 11.4 % and improved AUC from 0.71 to 0.76. Cross-validation over five disjoint school cohorts confirmed stability. The paper also provides identifiability conditions under which the prior-informed model is distinguishable from the standard formulation.

It is about: researcher Emilija Zec (R0322) and company Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002), challenge C002-CH1.

Claims:

2. Emilija Zec and Zrenjanin Game Works would apply mixture IRT and Bayesian knowledge tracing with slip and guess priors to the company's clickstream logs, producing an interpretable per-student guessing-probability flag that teachers can act on before the 2025–26 school year. [C002-CH1, SYN-PUB-03988, SYN-PUB-02526, SYN-PUB-03983, SYN-PUB-03989, R0322]

4. The challenge requires that the flagging method explain what it is doing so that teachers can act on it, and the company would not trust a method that does not do so. [C002-CH1]

Teachers tell us our math games are fun but they can't see whether a child is actually learning — we have clickstream data for 4,200 students but no way to tell if a pupil is guessing randomly versus genuinely understanding the material.

Every time a child clicks an answer in our math games, we log it — timestamp, question ID, answer chosen, how long they took, how many attempts. We have that data for about 4,200 students across the 2022–23 and 2023–24 school years. The problem is we have no way to read anything meaningful out of it. Review the claims of proposal C006-CH1-R0484.
It is about: researcher Jovan Puzović (R0484) and company PravniPilot a.d. (C006), challenge C006-CH1.

Claims:
1. A corpus of over two million published court decisions, indexed in PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch, covering courts whose customers operate in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. [C006]
2. PravniPilot's model achieves 61% accuracy; internal fine-tuning experiments have not moved accuracy past 63%, and the company targets 75% accuracy on a held-out test set within 12 months. [C006-CH1]
3. The company has processed over two million court decisions and indexes them using PostgreSQL and Elasticsearch. [C006]

Sources:
[C006] company · PravniPilot a.d. · 2012 · company C006
PravniPilot a.d. (C006): Legal tech, Subotica, 78 employees, founded 2012.
PravniPilot a.d. was founded in 2012 in Subotica by a small team of practicing lawyers and software developers who were tired of spending hours manually searching court archives. We started with a simple keyword-search tool for Serbian civil cases and, over twelve years, grew that into a full AI-assisted research and case-prediction platform now used by 230 law firms in Serbia, Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Our platform ingests published court decisions, extracts key legal arguments, and gives lawyers a structured view of how similar disputes have been decided. The prediction module estimates probable outcome ranges for commercial, labor, and property disputes. We do not replace legal judgment — we give lawyers faster access to better evidence so their judgment is better informed. Our development office sits inside NTP Novi Sad, where most of our engineering and data team works. The Subotica headquarters handles commercial, finance and client relations. Across both offices we employ 78 people, roughly half of them with legal backgrounds. Our current customers range from two-partner boutique firms in Banja Luka to mid-size litigation practices in Zagreb and Belgrade. …[+3573 chars]

Review the claims of pair C002-CH2:R0207.
It is about: researcher Danijela Fejsa (R0207) and company Zrenjanin Game Works d.o.o. (C002), challenge C002-CH2.

Claims:
1. The researcher co-authored work on colour contrast and background complexity effects on reading speed and comprehension for students with visual processing difficulties (SYN-PUB-02651). [SYN-PUB-02651]
2. Danijela Fejsa led the work package responsible for development and validation of an accessibility assessment framework in the ADRIADL project, coordinating with educational institutions in Serbia, Hungary, and Croatia (SYN-PRJ-0079). [SYN-PRJ-0079]
3. Danijela Fejsa and Zrenjanin Game Works would design and run a classroom-based study comparing font types, colour contrast levels, and text-presentation speeds on reading performance in children with suspected reading difficulties (C002-CH2), drawing on colour contrast and background complexity research (SYN-PUB-02651) and UDL-based digital learning accessibility methods (SYN-PRJ-0078), to produce evidence-backed recommendations implementable in one update cycle (C002-CH2). [C002-CH2, SYN-PUB-02651, SYN-PRJ-0078]
4. The company's user population is identified only by informal teacher reports, not formal diagnosis (C002-CH2). [C002-CH2]
5. Miroslav Kovačević is available for roughly one day per week for research-related work, and Tatjana Kovačević is available for pedagogy input on a similar basis, with both constrained by ongoing contract delivery (C002). [C002]

Sources:

Review the claims of profile R0207.
It is about: researcher Danijela Fejsa (R0207).

Claims:
1. Led a work package in the ADRIADL project responsible for empirical validation of an accessibility assessment framework across Serbian pilot schools. [SYN-PRJ-0079]

Sources:
[SYN-PRJ-0079] project · Accessible Digital Learning across the Adriatic–Danube Region: Framework Development and Pilot Validation · 2019 · researchers R0207, R1043
ADRIADL: Accessible Digital Learning across the Adriatic–Danube Region: Framework Development and Pilot Validation (Interreg IPA Hungary–Serbia, 2019–2022).
Participants: R0207 work package leader; R1043 team member.
Partners: Faculty of Education in Sombor, University of Novi Sad; University of Pécs, Faculty of Informatics, Hungary; Faculty of Teacher Education, University of Rijeka, Croatia; National Institute of Education Research, Budapest, Hungary.
ADRIADL brought together educational research institutions in Serbia, Hungary, and Croatia to develop a shared framework for assessing and improving the accessibility of digital instructional materials in primary education. Fejsa led the work package responsible for empirical validation of the framework across Serbian pilot schools, coordinating a team of four researchers who conducted classroom observations, student assessments, and teacher interviews in 14 schools. The project produced a trilingual framework document, a validated teacher self-assessment instrument available in Serbian, Hungarian, and Croatian, and a series of open-access training videos. Findings were disseminated through national teacher in-service training networks in all three partner countries.

This book chapter reviews the application of vibration-based SHM to steel civil and industrial structures, with emphasis on welded connections. The chapter covers the theoretical basis of modal analysis, sensor placement strategies, algorithm selection criteria, and the practical challenges of long-term monitoring including power supply, data transmission, and environmental compensation. Review the claims of profile R0995.
It is about: researcher Veljko Pantelić (R0995).

Claims:
1. Metamodel and Xtext-based parser infrastructure for IEC 61131-3 Structured Text targeting programmable logic controllers, including grammar specification, conformance checking, and IDE support. [SYN-PUB-10372, SYN-PUB-10375]
2. Software product-line engineering for PLC systems using FODA feature models, variability management, and binding-time analysis for configuration spaces of automation equipment families. [SYN-PUB-10374]
3. Has industry experience as a part-time software engineer during 2013–2015 at a Novi Sad-based automation integrator developing IEC 61131-3 programs for conveyor and palletiser systems. [R0995]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-10372] publication · A Metamodel for IEC 61131-3 Structured Text: Design Rationale and Conformance Checking · 2015 · researchers R0995
A Metamodel for IEC 61131-3 Structured Text: Design Rationale and Conformance Checking (2015, journal, Journal of Systems and Control Engineering Research).
Authors: Miroslav Đorđević (outside co-author); Veljko Pantelić (R0995); Tibor Farkaš (outside co-author).
Keywords: IEC 61131-3; Structured Text; metamodeling; Ecore; OCL; conformance checking.
IEC 61131-3 defines five programming languages for programmable logic controllers, yet no widely adopted formal metamodel exists for its Structured Text variant. This paper presents a metamodel covering the full grammar of Structured Text as defined in the third edition of the standard, implemented in Ecore within the Eclipse Modeling Framework. The metamodel comprises 47 metaclasses and 112 structural features. Conformance checking is realized through 34 OCL constraints covering type compatibility, scope resolution, and temporal execution order. The metamodel was validated against a corpus of 18 publicly available PLC project archives totalling approximately 120,000 lines of Structured Text, extracted from open automation repositories. Authors: Stefan Kostić (R0375); Milica Vujanović (outside co-author); Dragan Petrović (outside co-author).
Keywords: MC/DC coverage; embedded C; Frama-C; mutation testing; RTOS.
This paper examines three widely used structural coverage criteria—branch, decision, and modified condition/decision coverage (MC/DC)—as applied to embedded C programs running on microcontrollers with limited RAM and flash memory. We implemented a static instrumentation framework on top of Frama-C and evaluated it against a suite of 14 open-source RTOS driver modules totalling approximately 18,000 lines of code. Measurements were collected on an STM32-based hardware testbed. Our biochar product tests at around 55% fixed carbon but customers in Germany need at least 70% for soil-amendment certification; we've tried raising pyrolysis temperature but that cuts yield by nearly a third and makes the economics fall apart.

Our biochar consistently comes out with around 55% fixed carbon when we run the pyrolyser at 500–520 °C, which is where our yield is commercially acceptable. Buyers in Germany and the Netherlands need at least 70% fixed carbon to qualify under soil-amendment certification schemes. We have pushed the temperature up to 650 °C and beyond in trials, and we do hit the 70% threshold, but the mass yield drops from roughly 28% to under 20%, which means we need about 40% more raw material to fill the same order. At current feedstock and energy costs that wipes out the price premium we get for certified biochar. We have also tried extending the hold time at lower temperatures rather than raising the peak, but the gains in fixed carbon are modest. We have two years of batch logs covering temperature profiles, feedstock moisture, particle size and output quality that we can share. We need a way to improve fixed-carbon content without either wrecking yield or requiring capital we do not have for a new reactor. Comparison of Frequency-Domain Decomposition and Stochastic Subspace Identification for Damage Localization in Multi-Bay Steel Frames (2015, journal, Journal of Vibration Diagnostics and Structural Integrity).
Authors: Jelena Jokić (R0666); Dragan Milošević (outside co-author); Attila Varga (outside co-author).
Keywords: FDD; SSI-COV; damage index; multi-bay frame; damage localization.
Two widely used OMA algorithms—frequency-domain decomposition (FDD) and stochastic subspace identification (SSI-COV)—are compared for their ability to localize damage in a three-bay, two-storey welded steel frame model. Damage was simulated by progressively cutting a weld in the lower right column-beam connection in three stages, reducing net throat area by 20%, 40%, and 60%. Ambient excitation was provided by pedestrian-like loading applied at the floor levels. Both algorithms identified natural frequencies within 0.15 Hz of each other for the first six modes. Damage localization was assessed via the modal strain energy damage index (MSEDI). SSI-COV achieved correct panel identification at 20% damage in 7 of 10 repeated trials, while FDD achieved correct localization in only 4 of 10 at the same damage level. Review the claims of profile R0283.
It is about: researcher Ana Mamužić (R0283).

Claims:
1. EMC filter design for SiC MOSFET inverter drives with high-frequency conducted emissions arising from fast switching transitions. [SYN-PUB-03539, SYN-PUB-03543]

Sources:
[SYN-PUB-03539] publication · EMC Filter Design for SiC MOSFET-Based Motor Drives: Comparison with IGBT Baseline at 150 kHz–30 MHz · 2021 · researchers R0283
EMC Filter Design for SiC MOSFET-Based Motor Drives: Comparison with IGBT Baseline at 150 kHz–30 MHz (2021, conference, Proceedings of the 22nd European Conference on Power Electronics and Applications (EPE-ECCE Europe)).
Authors: Ana Mamužić (R0283); Nikola Đorđević (outside co-author); Thomas Berger (outside co-author).
Keywords: SiC MOSFET; IGBT comparison; rise time; high-frequency EMI; four-stage filter.
Silicon carbide MOSFET inverters switch at voltages and currents with rise times below 50 ns, generating significantly higher high-frequency conducted emissions than conventional IGBT-based drives of equivalent power rating. This work compares the conducted emission spectra of a 7.5 kW SiC MOSFET drive (switching at 50 kHz) and an IGBT baseline (switching at 8 kHz) under the same load, and documents the additional filter attenuation required to achieve IEC 61800-3 Category C2 compliance for the SiC case. The SiC drive exceeded the Category C2 quasi-peak limit by up to 22 dB in the 5–30 MHz band compared to 9 dB for the IGBT. An optimised four-stage LC filter reduced the worst-case exceedance to within the 6 dB safety margin, at the cost of a 40% increase in filter volume relative to the IGBT design. Measured and simulated spectra agree within ±3 dB across the full range.

It is about: researcher Danijela Ninkov (R0611).

Claims:
1. Provides access to dedicated EMC laboratory equipped with LISN-based conducted emission measurement, power quality class A monitoring, network impedance characterisation up to 30 MHz, and a real-time power network emulator. [R0611]

Sources:
[R0611] researcher · Danijela Ninkov · researchers R0611
Danijela Ninkov (R0611): Full Professor, Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications, Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Electromagnetic Compatibility; Power Electronics; Power Systems and Power Quality; Signal Processing in Electrical Engineering.
Keywords: electromagnetic compatibility; conducted emissions; time-domain modelling; low-voltage power networks; power electronic loads; harmonic distortion; line impedance stabilisation network; grid-connected inverters; power quality; conducted disturbance propagation.
Bio: Danijela Ninkov received her Dipl.Ing. and M.Sc. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, in 1998 and 2003 respectively, and her Ph.D. from the same institution in 2008. She has held a Full Professor position since 2019 in the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications. Her research group focuses on electromagnetic compatibility in low-voltage distribution networks, with particular attention to time-domain modelling of conducted disturbances, harmonic propagation, and the interaction between power electronic loads and grid regulation equipment. She teaches undergraduate and postgraduate courses in electromagnetic compatibility and power quality. Review the claims of profile R1008.
It is about: researcher Krisztina Kiss (R1008).

Claims:
1. Protocol-agnostic anomaly detection for industrial control systems using byte-level payload features and one-class classification methods. [SYN-PUB-10483, SYN-PUB-10477]
2. Lightweight model compression for embedded ICS gateways through quantisation and structured pruning of autoencoder-based detectors. [SYN-PUB-10239]
3. Multi-protocol anomaly detection with score aggregation strategies including Dempster-Shafer combination and learned linear fusion for simultaneous monitoring of Modbus, DNP3, and EtherNet/IP traffic. [SYN-PUB-10482]

5. Incremental online learning with Gaussian mixture models and Bayesian updates for concept drift adaptation in continuous ICS traffic streams. [SYN-PUB-00492]
6. Threshold calibration for anomaly detectors under deployment conditions using unlabelled operational data and beta mixture models. [SYN-PUB-10480]
7. Statistical characterisation of industrial Ethernet traffic including long-range dependence, periodicity, and protocol-specific behaviour patterns in Modbus, DNP3, and EtherNet/IP networks. [SYN-PUB-10474, SYN-PUB-10473]
8. Evaluation of OPC UA encryption modes and their impact on traffic-based anomaly detection discriminability. [SYN-PUB-10478]
9. Open to joint projects with companies deploying ICS monitoring solutions, contract research on protocol traffic analysis and deployment, and consulting on detector calibration and deployment architecture. [R1008]
10. Open to supervising industrial PhDs for candidates from companies in automation and critical infrastructure. [R1008]

[R0611] researcher · Danijela Ninkov · researchers R0611
Danijela Ninkov (R0611): Full Professor, Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications, Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad.
Fields: Electromagnetic Compatibility; Power Electronics; Power Systems and Power Quality; Signal Processing in Electrical Engineering.
Keywords: electromagnetic compatibility; conducted emissions; time-domain modelling; low-voltage power networks; power electronic loads; harmonic distortion; line impedance stabilisation network; grid-connected inverters; power quality; conducted disturbance propagation.
Bio: Danijela Ninkov received her Dipl.Ing. and M.Sc. degrees in Electrical Engineering from the Faculty of Technical Sciences, University of Novi Sad, in 1998 and 2003 respectively, and her Ph.D. from the same institution in 2008. She has held a Full Professor position since 2019 in the Department of Power, Electronics and Telecommunications. Her research group focuses on electromagnetic compatibility in low-voltage distribution networks, with particular attention to time-domain modelling of conducted disturbances, harmonic propagation, and the interaction between power electronic loads and grid regulation equipment. She teaches undergraduate and postgraduate courses in electromagnetic compatibility and power quality. The group operates a dedicated EMC measurement laboratory equipped with a line impedance stabilisation network, conducted emission analysers calibrated to CISPR standards, and a real-time power network emulator.

Lines to translate:
1. Формална верификација протокола за испоруку фирмвера методом провере модела (2013, conference, Зборник радова Телекомуникациони форум ТЕЛФОР).
2. Keywords: формална верификација; SPIN; Promelamodel checking; firmware protocol; LTL.
3. У овом раду примењен је алат за проверу модела SPIN на протокол за аутентификовану испоруку фирмвера у бежичним телеметријским мрежама. Протокол је моделован у Прометеловом језику, а верификација је обухватила 14 безбедносних и животних особина формулисаних у линеарној темпоралној логици. Пронађена су три услова у којима поновна репродукција старе поруке може да доведе до инсталације претходне верзије фирмвера ако је монотони бројач секвенце нулиран након ресетовања уређаја. Предложено је проширење протокола са тrajnim бројачем у заштићеном нелетљивом меморијском простору. Исправљени протокол је верификован без кршења постављених особина у простору стања са до 2,1 × 10⁸ стања. Рад такође дискутује ограничења апстракције криптографских примитива у SPIN моделу и предлаже методологију за раздвојено моделовање протоколне логике и криптографских претпоставки.

The protocol was modelled in the Promela language, and the verification covered 14 security and liveness properties formulated in linear temporal logic. Three conditions were found in which replay of an old message can lead to the installation of a previous firmware version if the monotonic sequence counter is reset after a device reset. An extension of the protocol with a persistent counter in a protected non-volatile memory area is proposed. The corrected protocol was verified without violation of the stated properties in a state space of up to 2.1 × 10⁸ states. Teachers tell us our math games are fun but they can't see whether a child is actually learning — we have clickstream data for 4,200 students but no way to tell if a pupil is guessing randomly versus genuinely understanding the material.

Every time a child clicks an answer in our math games, we log it — timestamp, question ID, answer chosen, how long they took, how many attempts. We have that data for about 4,200 students across the 2022–23 and 2023–24 school years. The problem is we have no way to read anything meaningful out of it. A teacher told us last spring that one of her students had a 91% score but she was convinced the child understood nothing and was just clicking fast until something turned green. She was right — when she tested the child on paper the results were very different. We know this is a real problem but we do not know how to separate genuine learning from lucky guessing using the data we already have. We have exported the logs to CSV and tried building simple accuracy thresholds ourselves, but that does not catch the fast random clicker.
